title: Choosing between cash flows
objectives: Compare two streams of cash flows by net present value.

screens.prose: A project costs £1,000.00 today. It pays back £550.00 in 1 year and £550.00 in 2 years. Money left elsewhere earns 10% a year.
screens.question: Should you take the project?

options.text: Yes: it pays back £100.00 more than it costs
options.why: You added £1,100.00 back against £1,000.00 out. Paid later, the £1,100.00 is worth only £954.55 today.

options.text: No: what it pays back is worth less than £1,000.00 today
There is no way to tell
options.why: We can tell: discount each payment at 10%, then compare with the £1,000.00.

hints.text: What is each payment worth today at 10%?
Discount the year 1 payment once and the year 2 payment twice.

feedback.correct: The payments are worth £954.55 today, below the £1,000.00 cost.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Value both payments today, then compare with the cost.

explain.text: Today the payments are worth $\tfrac{550}{1.1} + \tfrac{550}{1.1^2} = 500 + 454.55 = 954.55$. That is £45.45 short of the cost. Left at 10%, your £1,000.00 would beat the project.

screens.prose: Count the cost as a negative cash flow, then add every present value. Slide the rate and watch the total, P.

derive.caption: Rate {{fixed(r * 100, 1)}}%: total today {{money(-1000 + 550 / pow(1 + r, 1) + 550 / pow(1 + r, 2))}}

screens.question: Slide the rate to 0%. What is the total?

hints.text: Slide the rate all the way left.
At 0% nothing is discounted.

feedback.correct: At 0% the total is the plain sum, £100.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the rate to 0% and read the caption.

byKey.no-cost: You left out the £1,000.00 cost. It counts as a negative cash flow.
byKey.ten: That is the total at 10%. Slide the rate down to 0%.

explain.text: At 0% the total is the plain sum, $-1000 + 550 + 550 = 100$. Every higher rate pulls it down. It crosses zero between 6% and 7%.

screens.prose: That total is the **net present value**, or NPV: every present value added, the cost counted as negative. A desk spends £5,000.00 on a model that saves £2,000.00 a year for 3 years. The rate is 8%.
screens.question: Fill in the present values and the NPV, in pounds.

hints.text: Multiply each cash flow by its factor.
The NPV adds all four present values, including −£5,000.00.

feedback.correct: NPV £154.19: positive, so the model beats leaving the money at 8%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each cash flow by its factor, then add all four, the cost included.

byKey.r4c3: Add all four present values. The −£5,000.00 is one of them.

explain.text: The savings are worth £5,154.19 today, so the NPV is £154.19. A positive NPV means the project beats the 8% available elsewhere. The rule: accept a project when its NPV is positive.

screens.prose: The NPV depends on the rate. Here is the desk's model again, with its NPV plotted against the rate.
screens.question: Drag the slider until the NPV is zero. At what rate does that happen?

hints.text: Watch P cross the horizontal line at zero.
At 8% the NPV is £154.19, still positive. Go higher.
The NPV reaches zero at about 9.7%.

feedback.correct: About 9.70%: there the savings are worth exactly £5,000.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move the slider until P sits on the zero line.

byKey.low: At that rate the NPV is still above zero. Move right.
byKey.high: The NPV is below zero there. Move left.

explain.text: The NPV hits zero at about 9.70%. That rate is the **internal rate of return**, or IRR. Solving for it exactly needs Newton's method, from Series and Approximation.

screens.prose: Two projects each cost £1,000.00. A pays £1,331.00 in year 3. B pays £800.00, £300.00 and £100.00 over years 1 to 3. Slide the rate and compare their NPVs.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: A wins at 4%, B wins at 8%
A wins at every rate, because it pays more in total
options.why: Its £1,331.00 comes last, so discounting hits it hardest. At 8%, B's NPV is £77.33 and A's £56.59.

options.text: B wins at every rate, because it pays sooner
options.why: At 4%, A's NPV is £183.25 against B's £135.50. Late cash matters less when rates are low.
The curves cross only once, near 6.7%. Elsewhere one is above the other.

hints.text: Set 4%, then 8%, and read both NPVs.
The curves cross between 6% and 7%.

feedback.correct: The ranking flips where the curves cross, near 6.7%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read both NPVs at 4% and at 8%.

explain.text: The curves cross near 6.7%. Below it, A's larger total wins; above it, B's earlier cash wins. A ranking by NPV holds only at the rate it was computed at.

screens.prose: A deal pays £300.00 at the end of each of the next 4 years, for £1,100.00 today. Your other investments earn 7%. A colleague says: £1,200.00 comes back, so the deal makes £100.00.
screens.question: What is the deal's NPV at 7%?

hints.text: Discount each £300.00 for its own wait.
The four factors at 7% add to 3.3872.

feedback.correct: NPV −£83.84: the deal loses value at 7%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount each payment for its own wait, add them, then take away £1,100.00.

byKey.undisc: You added the cash without discounting, as the colleague did. Each £300.00 is worth less the later it comes.
byKey.no-cost: £1,016.16 is the value of the payments. Take away the £1,100.00 cost.
byKey.once: You discounted all £1,200.00 by one year. The later payments wait longer.
byKey.last: You discounted all £1,200.00 by four years. Only the last payment waits that long.

explain.text: The payments are worth $300(\tfrac{1}{1.07} + \tfrac{1}{1.07^2} + \tfrac{1}{1.07^3} + \tfrac{1}{1.07^4}) = 1016.16$ today. So the NPV is −£83.84. Summing undiscounted cash ignores when it arrives.

screens.prose: You discounted each cash flow for its own wait and added, the outlay included. With $C_t$ paid at time $t$, $$NPV(r) = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}$$ Accept when $NPV > 0$. The IRR is the rate where $NPV(r) = 0$.
screens.question: In the sum, what is the $t = 0$ term?

options.why: You discounted the outlay by a year. It is paid today, and $(1 + r)^0 = 1$.

options.text: There is none: the outlay is left out
options.why: Leaving the outlay out gives the value of what comes back, not the net gain.

hints.text: What is $(1 + r)^0$?

feedback.correct: $\frac{C_0}{(1 + r)^0} = C_0$: the outlay counts in full.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $t = 0$ into $\frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}$.

explain.text: At $t = 0$ the factor is $(1 + r)^0 = 1$, so the term is $C_0$ itself. For the desk's model, $C_0 = -5000$. A negative $C_0$ is what makes the NPV net.

screens.title: NPV in Python
screens.prose: The desk wants NPV as a function. `flows[0]` is paid today, `flows[1]` in a year, and so on. The rate is a decimal, so 8% is `0.08`.
screens.question: Complete `npv(rate, flows)` in plain Python.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests, including a 0% rate and a single cash flow paid today. Each answer is accepted when math.isclose(actual, expected, rel_tol=1e-9).

hints.text: Each term is `cash` divided by $(1 + r)^t$.
`enumerate` gives `t = 0` for the first cash flow, so it is not discounted.
Replace `...` with `cash / (1 + rate) ** t`.

feedback.correct: One line of discounting covers every stream.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Each term should be `cash / (1 + rate) ** t`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that the `...` is replaced.

explain.text:
The loop discounts each cash flow for its own wait, $t$ years. Because `t` starts at 0, the outlay is not discounted. `npv(0.08, [-5000, 2000, 2000, 2000])` returns 154.19, as in your table.

```python
total += cash / (1 + rate) ** t
```

screens.prose: A bond costs £95.00. It pays £4.00 at the end of each year for 3 years, and £100.00 back with the last payment. Your required return is 5%.

state.caption: Buying the bond: cash out today, cash in later

screens.question: What is the NPV of buying the bond at 5%?

hints.text: The last cash flow is £104.00: a coupon plus the £100.00.
The three payments are worth £97.28 today.

feedback.correct: NPV £2.28: buy, because the bond returns more than 5%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount £4.00, £4.00 and £104.00 for 1, 2 and 3 years, then take away £95.00.

byKey.undisc: You added the cash without discounting. Each payment is worth less the later it comes.
byKey.no-cost: £97.28 is the value of the payments. Take away the £95.00 price.
byKey.no-principal: You left out the £100.00 repaid in year 3. The last cash flow is £104.00.

explain.text: The payments are worth £97.28 today, £2.28 more than the price. So buying at £95.00 earns more than 5%: its IRR is 5.87%. In Pricing a bond, £97.28 becomes the bond's fair price at 5%.

screens.prose: A trading desk can buy a faster data feed for £130,000.00 today. It should cut slippage by £50,000.00 a year for 3 years. The firm's rate is 7%.
screens.question: What is the feed's NPV at 7%?

hints.text: Discount each £50,000.00 for its own wait.
The three factors at 7% add to 2.624316.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount each year's saving at 7%, add them, then take away the cost.

byKey.undisc: You added the cash without discounting. Three years of savings are worth less than £150,000.00 today.
byKey.no-cost: That is the value of the savings. Take away the £130,000.00 cost.
byKey.at8: That is the NPV at 8%. The firm's rate is 7%.

explain.text: The savings are worth £131,215.80 today, so the NPV is £1,215.80. The IRR is 7.51%, so at 8% the answer flips to −£1,145.15. With a margin this thin, the slippage estimate matters more than the arithmetic.

ideas: The NPV adds every cash flow's present value, the outlay counted as a negative cash flow today.
Accept a project when its NPV is positive. The rate that makes the NPV zero is the IRR.
NPV falls as the rate rises, and two streams can rank differently at different rates. At 0% the NPV is the plain sum.

formula.name: Net present value
formula.note: $C_0$ is the outlay, usually negative, and is not discounted.

summary.trap: Summing cash flows without discounting, or ranking NPVs computed at different rates.

quiz.prose: A project costs £200.00 today and pays £120.00 at the end of each of the next 2 years. The rate is 5%.
quiz.question: What is its NPV?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount both payments, add them, then take away £200.00.

byKey.undisc: You added the cash without discounting. Later payments are worth less today.
byKey.no-cost: That is the value of the payments. Take away the £200.00 cost.

explain.text: The payments are worth $114.29 + 108.84 = 223.13$ today. Take away the £200.00 outlay: NPV £23.13. Positive, so accept.

quiz.prose: An analyst reports project A's NPV as £50.00 at 6%, and project B's as £70.00 at 9%. Both are risky in the same way.
quiz.question: What can you conclude?

options.text: B is better: its NPV is higher
options.why: You compared NPVs taken at different rates. B's NPV at 6% would be higher than £70.00.

options.text: A is better: it uses the lower rate
options.why: The rate is not a score. A lower rate simply raises every NPV.

options.text: Nothing yet: compute both at the same rate

feedback.correct: Rank projects only by NPVs at one shared rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the two NPVs are measured the same way.

explain.text: An NPV changes with the rate, so the two numbers are not comparable. Recompute both at the rate that fits their shared risk. Even then, rankings can flip at another rate.

quiz.prose: A stream is −£500.00 today, then £200.00 at the end of each of the next 3 years.
quiz.question: What is its NPV at a rate of 0%?

feedback.correct: At 0% the NPV is the plain sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. At 0% every factor is 1.

byKey.no-cost: You left out the −£500.00 paid today.

explain.text: At $r = 0$ every factor $(1 + 0)^{-t}$ is 1. So the NPV is the plain sum: $-500 + 600 = 100$. Any positive rate gives less.

quiz.prose: A project's NPV is £40.00 at 8% and −£25.00 at 10%.
quiz.question: Where is its IRR?

options.why: Below 8% the NPV is even higher than £40.00, so it cannot be zero there.
Above 10% the NPV falls further below −£25.00.
The NPV changes sign between 8% and 10%, so it passes through zero.

feedback.correct: The NPV changes sign between 8% and 10%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The IRR is where the NPV crosses zero.

explain.text: NPV falls as the rate rises, from £40.00 at 8% to −£25.00 at 10%. So it crosses zero in between. Straight-line interpolation guesses $8\% + 2\% \times \tfrac{40}{65} = 9.23\%$.
